name: Fluoxetine + Olanzapine (Symbyax)
summary: Combination of an SSRI antidepressant and an atypical antipsychotic for bipolar depression and treatment-resistant major depression. Powerful for mood, but carries significant metabolic, neurologic, and suicidality risks.
description: Olanzapine/fluoxetine (Symbyax) combines an SSRI (fluoxetine) with an atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine) in a single capsule. It’s used for acute bipolar I depression and for treatment-resistant major depressive disorder after other antidepressants have failed. It can be life-changing for some patients but often causes weight gain, metabolic changes, sedation, and hormonal side effects. It carries a suicidality warning in younger patients and a mortality warning in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Dosing is usually once nightly due to sedation.
patient_summary: Symbyax is a single capsule that combines Prozac (fluoxetine) and Zyprexa (olanzapine). It’s mainly used when depression is severe, bipolar, or has not responded to other antidepressants. Many people notice better sleep, less hopelessness, and more emotional stability, but there’s a tradeoff: weight gain, appetite changes, fatigue, and metabolic issues are common. You’ll need regular lab work and close monitoring for mood changes, especially early on.

metadata.controlled_substance: Not a controlled substance (US), but high-risk for metabolic and neurologic adverse effects

primary_indications: Acute depressive episodes in Bipolar I Disorder

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for acute bipolar I depressive episodes. Often considered when first-line mood stabilizer plus antidepressant strategies are insufficient or poorly tolerated.
FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression after failure of at least 2 antidepressant trials in the current episode.
Used when standard antidepressants alone have not worked. Provides multimodal serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine effects via combined SSRI and antipsychotic mechanisms.
Not approved for dementia-related psychosis; antipsychotic use in this population increases mortality and cerebrovascular event risk.

contraindications: Current use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) intended to treat psychiatric disorders or use within 14 days of discontinuing an MAOI
Initiation of olanzapine/fluoxetine within 5 weeks of discontinuing fluoxetine or the combination (due to long half-life)
Use with pimozide or thioridazine (QT prolongation and serious arrhythmia risk; thioridazine should not be started until 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine)
Concurrent or recent (within 5 weeks) use with IV methylene blue
Known hypersensitivity or prior serious reaction (eg, DRESS, anaphylaxis) to olanzapine, fluoxetine, or any component
Use in patients with dementia-related psychosis (boxed mortality warning; not approved for this indication)

efficacy_response.metric: Depression response rate at ~8 weeks in bipolar I depression and treatment-resistant depression
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Response rates are generally higher than placebo and higher than antidepressant monotherapy in treatment-resistant depression, but with more metabolic and weight-related side effects.
efficacy_response.patient_text: In studies, many people with bipolar depression or very stubborn unipolar depression had meaningful improvement in mood, energy, and functioning over 1 to 2 months on olanzapine/fluoxetine—especially after other antidepressants had failed. The flip side is a high rate of weight gain and metabolic changes, so labs and lifestyle support are not optional.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Efficacy estimates synthesized from clinical trial data comparing olanzapine/fluoxetine with placebo and standard antidepressants.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally; not significantly affected by food. Given once daily, typically at night due to sedating effects of olanzapine.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: High oral bioavailability for both components (olanzapine and fluoxetine).
pharmacokinetics.onset: Sleep and appetite often change within days; mood and energy typically require several weeks.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Olanzapine: ~5–8 hours; Fluoxetine: ~6–8 hours after a dose.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Olanzapine: ~20–50 hours; Fluoxetine: ~2–4 days; active metabolite (norfluoxetine): ~7–15 days.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Clinical effect persists through 24 hours with once-daily dosing due to long half-lives.
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Not applicable for this specific combination product (no extended-release Symbyax formulation).
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Olanzapine: primarily hepatic via CYP1A2 and glucuronidation; Fluoxetine: hepatic via CYP2D6 and other pathways to active norfluoxetine.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Renal and fecal elimination of metabolites; unchanged parent drug excretion is minimal.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Both components are highly protein bound.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken with or without food; evening dosing helps with sedation and GI tolerability.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Olanzapine/fluoxetine (Symbyax) is not a first-line antidepressant. It’s a heavier-hitting option used when standard treatments aren’t enough or when depression is part of bipolar I disorder.
items: Bipolar I depression: Acute depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder, especially when symptoms are severe, disabling, or associated with suicidality.
Treatment-resistant depression (TRD): Major depressive episodes that have not responded to at least 2 adequate trials of different antidepressants in the current episode.
Evening dosing: Usually taken at night because olanzapine is sedating and can increase appetite.
off_label: Not typically used off-label beyond its approved indications; other antipsychotic/antidepressant strategies are preferred for most off-label situations.
Not appropriate for behavioral symptoms of dementia-related psychosis due to increased mortality and stroke risk.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Experiences with Symbyax are often "strong" in both directions—when it helps, it can help a lot, but the side effects can also be very real. Here’s what patients commonly describe:

quotes: It didn’t fix my life overnight, but the crushing hopelessness loosened its grip.
I noticed I wasn’t crying every day and I wasn’t stuck in bed until noon.
The world felt a little less heavy. Still had bad days, but they weren’t all bad.
The first few nights I was out cold within an hour—almost too sedated.
I finally slept through the night, but I was groggy in the morning.
If I take it too late, I’m a zombie the next day.
My appetite went from ‘meh’ to ‘I could eat everything in the fridge.’
The mood lift was great, but the weight gain freaked me out.
I felt better emotionally but had to buy new pants after a few months.
items.note: Weight gain and metabolic changes are VERY common. This is not a side effect to ignore—labs and lifestyle support matter.

quotes: My thoughts weren’t racing as much, but I felt slower mentally.
I didn’t feel as desperately sad, but I also felt a bit emotionally flat.
I could focus enough to get through work, but I definitely felt more sluggish.
My sex drive basically disappeared.
Periods got weird—heavier some months, then barely there.
No one told me my hormones could be affected this much.
items.note: Hyperprolactinemia and sexual side effects can show up as menstrual changes, breast changes, low libido, or sexual dysfunction.

quotes: The first 1–2 weeks were rough—nausea, feeling off, and weirdly restless.
I felt both sleepy and restless at the same time. It eventually smoothed out.
My anxiety blipped up a bit before it settled down.
I started feeling more agitated and ‘amped’ instead of calmer.
I had scary thoughts about not wanting to be alive that I didn’t have before.
The weight gain and fatigue became deal-breakers, even though my mood improved.
items.note: Any new or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe agitation, mania-like symptoms, or rapid weight gain are red-flag reasons to call your prescriber ASAP.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: This is not a quick PRN medication. It’s a daily mood treatment that builds in your system over time. One component (fluoxetine) has a very long half-life, so changes in dose take days to weeks to fully show up.
key_points: First week: Sleep and appetite often change first. Some people feel sedated, others feel a bit activated or restless.
2–4 weeks: Early mood benefits may show up—less hopelessness, fewer crying spells, better ability to get out of bed and function.
4–8 weeks: Full antidepressant effect is typically evaluated. If there’s going to be a meaningful response, clinicians usually see it by this window.
All day coverage: Once-daily dosing provides 24-hour coverage because both drugs have long half-lives.
Long tail: Fluoxetine and its metabolite linger for weeks after discontinuation, so side effects and interactions can persist after you stop.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Response Rate in Severe or Treatment-Resistant Depression
sections.comparison: Higher response than placebo and higher than antidepressant alone in treatment-resistant depression, at the cost of significant metabolic side effects.
sections.text: Olanzapine/fluoxetine sits in the “heavy artillery” category: it’s not the first thing we reach for, but when standard antidepressants have failed or when bipolar depression is severe, this combination can move the needle. The tradeoff is that the same olanzapine that boosts mood stability also drives weight gain, cholesterol changes, and blood sugar problems in a sizable chunk of patients.
sections.clinical_details: Across clinical trials, the combination of olanzapine and fluoxetine generally shows higher response and remission rates than either agent alone or placebo in bipolar I depression and treatment-resistant major depressive disorder. Clinical improvement typically emerges within 2–4 weeks and is assessed more formally by 6–8 weeks. Clinicians must weigh benefits against substantial risks of metabolic syndrome, sedation, and extrapyramidal symptoms, especially in long-term use.

citation.title: Combination olanzapine/fluoxetine therapy in bipolar depression and treatment-resistant major depressive disorder

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Black box warnings: (1) Increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. (2) Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults. This risk does not appear increased in adults over 24 and may be reduced in adults 65 and older. Monitor all patients closely—especially in the first 1–2 months and around dose changes. Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at increased risk of death. Olanzapine/fluoxetine is NOT approved for dementia-related psychosis.
other: New or worsening suicidal thoughts, self-harm, or dramatic mood swings require urgent evaluation.
Not approved in children younger than 10 years.
High risk for weight gain, elevated cholesterol, and elevated triglycerides—may contribute to diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
Can increase blood sugar, sometimes severely (including ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar states).
Can raise prolactin, leading to menstrual changes, breast changes, or sexual dysfunction.
May cause movement disorders (restlessness, tremor, stiffness, or tardive dyskinesia).
Risk of serious reactions like neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), DRESS (multiorgan hypersensitivity), and serotonin syndrome.
May cause orthostatic hypotension—dizziness or fainting when standing.
May prolong QT interval (fluoxetine) and alter cardiac conduction, especially with other QT-prolonging drugs.
Abrupt discontinuation of the antipsychotic or SSRI components can cause withdrawal and symptom rebound.
patient_counseling: You and your family should watch closely for new or worse suicidal thoughts, severe agitation, panic, or dramatic mood swings—especially in the first 1–2 months. If these show up, call your prescriber or go to the ER.
This medication can cause significant weight gain and metabolic changes. Expect regular labs (glucose, A1C, lipids) and weight/BMI monitoring.
Report symptoms like high thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or unexplained fatigue—these can signal high blood sugar.
Tell your clinician about any menstrual changes, breast discharge, breast enlargement, or sexual side effects.
Seek emergency care for fever, muscle stiffness, confusion, or autonomic instability (possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome).
Seek urgent care for rash with fever, swollen lymph nodes, or organ symptoms (possible DRESS).
Avoid sudden discontinuation unless directed. Both mood symptoms and withdrawal symptoms can flare if stopped abruptly.
Avoid combining with other serotonergic meds or QT-prolonging meds without explicit prescriber guidance.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The big three with olanzapine/fluoxetine are: (1) weight gain and metabolic changes, (2) sedation and fatigue, and (3) hormonal and movement-related side effects. These can be dose-related and cumulative over time.
plain_language_list: Weight gain and increased appetite (very common, often >7% of baseline weight).
Increased cholesterol and triglycerides; decreased “good” HDL.
Sedation, drowsiness, and fatigue—especially early on or after dose increases.
Dry mouth, increased appetite, and GI changes (bloating, nausea, or indigestion).
Hormonal changes like increased prolactin (irregular periods, breast changes, sexual dysfunction).
Tremor, restlessness, or other movement symptoms in some people.
Changes in liver enzymes on blood tests.
Orthostatic dizziness or feeling lightheaded when standing up.

common.incidence: Very common (weight gain ≥7% of baseline; dyslipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia frequently reported in both adults and youth).
common.patient_note: This medication is notorious for increasing appetite and causing weight gain. It also raises cholesterol, triglycerides, and can push people toward prediabetes or diabetes. Plan from day one: nutrition, movement, and regular labs are part of treatment, not optional extras.

common.incidence: About 1 in 4 or more experience significant sedation.
common.patient_note: Many people feel very sleepy, especially at the beginning or after dose changes. Taking it at night helps. If you’re too groggy in the morning to function, talk with your prescriber about dose timing or adjustment.

common.incidence: Increased appetite and dry mouth reported in ~15–20% or more.
common.patient_note: You might find yourself constantly snacking or craving carbs, plus feeling like your mouth is a desert. Sugar-free gum, water, and structured meals can help—but the appetite effect can be powerful.

common.incidence: High rates of increased LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides; risk of hyperglycemia.
common.patient_note: These are usually silent—you don’t feel them until there’s a problem. That's why regular blood work matters. We’re not being annoying with labs; we’re trying to protect your heart and pancreas.

common.incidence: Common, especially in youth; prolactin elevation reported in a large proportion of patients.
common.patient_note: You may notice menstrual changes, breast tenderness or discharge, low libido, or sexual dysfunction. These are medication side effects, not “in your head,” and they’re important to bring up.

common.symptom: Tremor, Restlessness, and Other Movement Symptoms
common.incidence: Tremor and restlessness occur in a noticeable minority of patients.
common.patient_note: Some people feel jittery, can’t sit still (akathisia), or develop tremor or stiffness. These may be subtle early on. Report them quickly; dose changes or meds to counteract EPS may help.

serious: Suicidal thoughts or behaviors, particularly in children, adolescents, and young adults—requires close monitoring and may require dose change or discontinuation.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, muscle rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability—medical emergency.
Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, clonus, fever, diarrhea—especially with other serotonergic drugs; requires prompt discontinuation and urgent care.
DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms): rash, fever, swollen lymph nodes, organ dysfunction—can be life-threatening.
Severe hyperglycemia and diabetic complications (ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar states).
Significant hyponatremia/SIADH: confusion, headache, seizures, or falls—more common in older adults and those on diuretics.
QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias, particularly with other QT-prolonging agents or electrolyte disturbances.
Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible abnormal movements, especially with long-term use and in older adults.
Agranulocytosis, neutropenia, and other blood dyscrasias: unexplained infections, fever, or sore throat may be warning signs.
Venous thromboembolism (DVT, pulmonary embolism), sometimes serious or fatal.
Hepatic injury: significant elevations in liver enzymes, rare cases of serious liver disease.
Pulmonary issues like aspiration pneumonia or, rarely, pulmonary fibrosis, particularly in vulnerable populations.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Olanzapine/fluoxetine interacts with many other medications through serotonin effects, cardiac conduction (QT interval), bleeding risk, and cytochrome P450 metabolism. Always run interaction checks before adding new meds.

items.with: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) and IV Methylene Blue
items.risk: High risk of serotonin syndrome and hypertensive reactions.
items.action: Contraindicated. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting olanzapine/fluoxetine. Wait at least 5 weeks after stopping olanzapine/fluoxetine before starting an MAOI or methylene blue.

items.risk: Marked QT prolongation and risk of life-threatening arrhythmias.
items.action: Contraindicated. Thioridazine should not be started until 5 weeks after discontinuing fluoxetine or this combination.

items.with: Other Serotonergic Medications (triptans, SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, MAOIs, linezolid, St John’s wort, amphetamines)
items.risk: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, autonomic instability, neuromuscular changes, GI symptoms).
items.action: Avoid or use extreme caution. Educate patients on early signs of serotonin syndrome and instruct them to seek urgent care if symptoms appear.

items.with: Drugs that Prolong QT Interval (certain antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, methadone)
items.risk: Additive QT prolongation increases risk of torsade de pointes and sudden death.
items.action: Avoid high-risk combinations when possible. If necessary, correct electrolytes, obtain baseline and follow-up ECGs, and use the lowest effective doses.

items.risk: Fluoxetine impairs platelet aggregation and can increase bleeding risk, especially GI bleeding and postpartum hemorrhage.
items.action: Use caution; discuss bleeding risks, watch for bruising, nosebleeds, black stools, or blood in urine.

items.with: Other CNS Depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedative hypnotics, alcohol, antihistamines, muscle relaxants)
items.risk: Additive sedation, respiratory depression, falls, and cognitive impairment.
items.action: Use the lowest effective doses, avoid alcohol, and counsel on fall and driving risk. Reassess the need for multiple sedating medications.

items.with: CYP2D6 Inhibitors or Substrates (e.g., some SSRIs, TCAs, antipsychotics, codeine, tamoxifen)
items.risk: Fluoxetine is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor—can raise levels of other CYP2D6 substrates and reduce conversion of prodrugs like codeine and tamoxifen.
items.action: Review all meds for CYP2D6 substrates. Dose adjustments or alternative agents may be needed.

items.risk: Olanzapine is metabolized by CYP1A2; smokers may have lower levels and less effect, while inhibitors can increase levels.
items.action: Monitor for changes in response if the patient starts or stops smoking or adds/removes CYP1A2 modulators; dose adjustments may be needed.

items.risk: Increased risk of SIADH and hyponatremia with SSRIs.
items.action: Monitor sodium, especially in older adults and those with volume depletion or diuretic use.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Because Symbyax combines a long half-life SSRI with an antipsychotic, discontinuation needs to be deliberate. Suddenly stopping can cause withdrawal symptoms and mood destabilization, but fluoxetine’s long half-life can also create a “built-in” slow taper for the SSRI component.
key_points: Never stop abruptly without guidance, especially if you’ve been on it for months or years.

Olanzapine taper: Gradually reduce the dose over weeks to months to avoid rebound insomnia, agitation, mood worsening, and antipsychotic withdrawal symptoms (restlessness, GI upset, anxiety, flu-like symptoms).
Fluoxetine taper: Because of the long half-life, SSRI discontinuation symptoms are usually milder than with shorter-acting SSRIs, but mood symptoms can still return. Taper is still recommended.
Typical clinical approach: Reduce total daily dose by about 25% every 1–2 weeks, slowing the taper if significant withdrawal symptoms or mood relapse occur.
Switching strategies: If transitioning to another antidepressant or antipsychotic, be mindful that fluoxetine and norfluoxetine may persist for weeks and interact with the new medication.
Monitoring during taper: Watch for return of depressive symptoms, suicidality, hypomania/mania, or new anxiety and insomnia. Pause or slow the taper if symptoms spike.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Symbyax is usually taken once daily in the evening. Starting doses are modest, but usual target doses still carry real metabolic and neurologic risk, so the goal is the lowest effective dose, not “as high as tolerated.”

adult.bipolar_depression_initial: Olanzapine 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg PO once nightly. Consider starting at 3 mg / 25 mg nightly in patients prone to hypotension, with hepatic impairment, slower metabolism (female, nonsmoker), or high sensitivity to sedation.
adult.bipolar_depression_titration: Adjust based on response and tolerability; increase olanzapine in 3–6 mg steps and fluoxetine in 25 mg steps, no more frequently than every several days to a week.
adult.bipolar_depression_target: Usual range: olanzapine 6–12 mg / fluoxetine 25–50 mg PO once nightly. Safety of olanzapine doses >18 mg or fluoxetine >75 mg daily in combination has not been established.
adult.trd_initial: Olanzapine 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg PO once nightly appended to a history of at least 2 prior failed antidepressant trials in the current episode.
adult.trd_titration: Increase slowly based on mood response, sedation, weight, and metabolic labs. Adjust olanzapine and fluoxetine as above; titrate more cautiously in those with hepatic impairment or multiple comorbidities.
adult.trd_target: Usual range: olanzapine 6–18 mg / fluoxetine 25–50 mg PO once nightly. Avoid pushing past this range without subspecialty input due to metabolic and neurologic risks.
adult.switching_maoi: Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting olanzapine/fluoxetine. After stopping olanzapine/fluoxetine, wait at least 5 weeks before starting an MAOI due to fluoxetine’s long half-life.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Start at lower doses (olanzapine 3–6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg nightly) and titrate slowly; clearance is reduced and side effects may be amplified.
adult.renal_impairment: No routine adjustment in mild-to-severe renal impairment, but monitor more closely; comorbidities often increase sensitivity.
adult.elderly: Start low and go slow (e.g., olanzapine 3–6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg nightly). Avoid use for dementia-related behaviors. Monitor sodium, falls, and cognition closely.

sections.simple_explanation: Think of Symbyax as a night-time, long-acting mood medicine. We start at a modest dose, see how your sleep, mood, and side effects behave over a few weeks, and then carefully adjust. The goal is to get enough antidepressant and mood-stabilizing effect without letting weight, blood sugar, cholesterol, or movement side effects spiral out of control.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: This combination crosses the placenta and enters breast milk. It also hits multiple organ systems (metabolic, neurologic, hormonal), so extra caution is needed in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, and those with medical comorbidities.
sections.pregnancy: Both olanzapine and fluoxetine cross the placenta. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics or SSRIs can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, respiratory distress, feeding issues) and, rarely, persistent pulmonary hypertension. SSRIs have mixed data on congenital malformations; antipsychotics carry metabolic and weight-related risks that can compound pregnancy complications. Use only when the benefits of mood stabilization clearly outweigh fetal and obstetric risks, and ideally in coordination with perinatal psychiatry and obstetrics.
sections.lactation: Olanzapine and fluoxetine are excreted in breast milk. Infant exposure can lead to sedation, feeding difficulties, irritability, or poor weight gain. If treatment is essential and no safer alternatives are appropriate, use the lowest effective dose, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, weight changes, and developmental concerns, and coordinate care with pediatrics.
sections.pediatrics: Approved for bipolar I depression in children ≥10 years and adolescents. Not approved in children <10. Kids and teens are more prone to metabolic side effects (weight gain, lipid changes), hyperprolactinemia, and extrapyramidal symptoms. There is also a suicidality black box warning in younger patients. Use only when clearly indicated, with very close monitoring of weight, BMI, waist circumference, and labs.
sections.geriatrics: In adults ≥65, Symbyax is high-risk. Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk in dementia-related psychosis and can worsen cognition and falls. SSRIs and antipsychotics both increase SIADH/hyponatremia risk. If used (e.g., for severe bipolar depression), start at very low doses, monitor sodium, falls, gait, and cognition, and regularly reassess ongoing need.
sections.hepatic: Both components are hepatically metabolized. In hepatic impairment, start at the lowest dose (often olanzapine 3–6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg nightly) and titrate slowly with frequent monitoring for sedation, metabolic issues, and liver function abnormalities.
sections.renal: No standard dose adjustment is required in renal impairment, but comorbidities (diabetes, cardiovascular disease) often magnify risks. Monitor metabolic parameters and volume status closely, and consider dose reductions if side effects emerge.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental health and suicidality: At every visit, assess mood, anxiety, suicidality, agitation, hypomania/mania, and overall functioning—especially in the first 1–2 months and after dose changes.
Adherence: Check at every visit. Nonadherence is common when side effects (weight gain, fatigue) show up before benefits.
Weight, BMI, and waist circumference: Baseline; then at 8 and 12 weeks, after dose changes, and at least quarterly. Consider more frequent checks early on.
Metabolic labs: Fasting glucose/A1C and lipid panel at baseline, ~4 months after initiation, and annually (more often if abnormal or high-risk).
Electrolytes and basic chemistries: At least annually; monitor sodium more closely in older adults, those on diuretics, or those with symptoms of hyponatremia.
CBC: As clinically indicated, and more frequently if history of low WBC or drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia; monitor for signs of infection.
Liver function tests: Baseline and periodically in long-term use, or if symptoms suggest liver problems (fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain).
ECG: Baseline and as clinically indicated in patients with cardiac disease, electrolyte abnormalities, or on other QT-prolonging medications.
Movement disorders (EPS and tardive dyskinesia): Assess at every visit; use a structured rating scale at least annually or every 6 months if higher risk.
Prolactin-related symptoms: Ask regularly about menstrual changes, libido, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, and sexual dysfunction; measure prolactin if symptoms are present.
Falls and gait: Especially in older adults—check for dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, and gait instability at each visit.
Signs of serotonin syndrome: New agitation, confusion, tremor, clonus, sweating, or diarrhea—especially when other serotonergic meds are present.
Global functioning: Track work/school performance, social functioning, and quality of life to ensure benefits outweigh side effects over time.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Symbyax comes as fixed-dose combination capsules. Lower or more flexible doses can be built using separate olanzapine and fluoxetine products when needed.
items: Symbyax capsules (brand): Olanzapine 3 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg; 6 mg / 25 mg.
Generic olanzapine/fluoxetine capsules: 3 mg / 25 mg; 6 mg / 25 mg; 6 mg / 50 mg; 12 mg / 25 mg; 12 mg / 50 mg.
Individual components (used when more flexible dosing is needed): Olanzapine tablets (multiple strengths) and fluoxetine capsules/tablets or liquid.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Olanzapine/fluoxetine works by hitting mood from two major angles at once. Fluoxetine is an SSRI that increases serotonin in synapses by blocking its reuptake. Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic that blocks multiple receptors, including serotonin (5-HT2A and 5-HT2C), dopamine (D2 and others), histamine (H1), and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, with moderate activity at muscarinic receptors. Together, they boost serotonin while modulating dopamine and other neurotransmitters. This combination can deepen antidepressant effects and stabilize mood in bipolar depression, but the same receptor actions drive weight gain, metabolic changes, sedation, and movement disorders.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In modern practice, olanzapine/fluoxetine is a second- or third-line option, not a starter antidepressant. For bipolar depression, first-line options often include mood stabilizers and other atypical antipsychotics with a more favorable metabolic profile. For treatment-resistant unipolar depression, clinicians usually try multiple strategies (different SSRIs/SNRIs, augmentation with lithium, other atypical antipsychotics, or psychotherapy) before arriving at this combination. Its role is usually reserved for situations where the depression is severe, clearly bipolar or treatment-resistant, and the patient and prescriber are willing to accept significant metabolic and weight risks in exchange for a higher chance of meaningful mood improvement. It should be avoided for dementia-related behaviors and used cautiously and time-limited in youth and older adults.

seo.title: Olanzapine/Fluoxetine (Symbyax): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, and Metabolic Risks
seo.description: Learn how Symbyax (olanzapine/fluoxetine) is used for bipolar depression and treatment-resistant depression, typical dosing ranges, serious metabolic and weight side effects, suicidality and dementia warnings, and what monitoring you actually need.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is Symbyax (olanzapine/fluoxetine) actually used for?
faqs.a: Symbyax is used for two main things: (1) acute depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder, and (2) treatment-resistant major depressive disorder—meaning depression that hasn’t responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials in the current episode. It’s not a first-line antidepressant for mild or moderate depression and should not be used for dementia-related behaviors.

faqs.q: How long does Symbyax take to work?
faqs.a: Sleep and appetite changes often show up within days. Mood and energy usually start to shift over 2–4 weeks, with full benefit often judged after 6–8 weeks. Because fluoxetine and its metabolite hang around for a long time, dose changes can take a couple of weeks to fully show up—this is a slow-steady medication, not an instant fix.

faqs.q: Is Symbyax good for anxiety or only depression?
faqs.a: The main targets are bipolar depression and treatment-resistant major depression. However, because it contains an SSRI (fluoxetine) and a sedating antipsychotic (olanzapine), anxiety symptoms often improve as mood stabilizes and sleep gets better. That said, it’s not usually chosen just for anxiety due to its heavy metabolic and neurologic side-effect profile.

Yes—this is one of the biggest downsides. Olanzapine is strongly associated with increased appetite, weight gain, and metabolic changes (increased triglycerides, cholesterol, and blood sugar). Many people gain more than 7% of their starting weight. If you use Symbyax, you need a proactive plan: nutrition, physical activity, regular weight/BMI checks, and lab monitoring (glucose/A1C and lipids).

faqs.q: What about diabetes and cholesterol—how worried should I be?
faqs.a: Concerned enough to take monitoring seriously. Symbyax can push people toward insulin resistance, high triglycerides, and high LDL cholesterol. Some patients with risk factors (family history, obesity) may develop diabetes. That’s why guidelines recommend baseline and follow-up fasting glucose or A1C and lipid panels, plus ongoing weight and waist measurements.

faqs.q: Can Symbyax make suicidal thoughts worse?
faqs.a: In children, adolescents, and young adults, antidepressants—including this combination—carry a black box warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors early in treatment or when doses change. For adults over 24, this risk does not appear increased overall, and adults over 65 may even have a reduced risk. Regardless of age, any new or worsening suicidal thoughts, self-harm behaviors, or severe agitation are red flags and need immediate attention.

They can, but it’s high risk and must be done very cautiously. In older adults, the antipsychotic component increases the risk of stroke, falls, metabolic issues, and overall mortality in those with dementia. SSRIs and antipsychotics also increase the risk of hyponatremia/SIADH. If an older adult needs Symbyax for severe bipolar depression or refractory depression, start at very low doses, monitor closely (including sodium and fall risk), and regularly reassess whether the benefits still justify the risks.

faqs.q: Is Symbyax the same as taking Prozac plus Zyprexa separately?
faqs.a: Pharmacologically, it’s the same drugs—fluoxetine and olanzapine—but in fixed-dose capsule combinations. Taking them separately can give more flexibility (for example, slightly different ratios or lower starting doses than the capsules allow), which is sometimes helpful in patients who are very sensitive to side effects. The fixed-dose combo is convenient but less customizable.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with Symbyax?
faqs.a: It’s strongly discouraged. Both components can cause sedation, and combining them with alcohol increases the risk of excessive drowsiness, poor judgment, falls, and accidents. Alcohol can also worsen mood and sleep, and may amplify metabolic issues. If you drink, talk honestly with your prescriber so you can make a realistic and safe plan.

faqs.q: Is Symbyax used for mania or psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Symbyax is approved for bipolar depression, not mania or mixed episodes. Using antidepressants in mania or mixed states can actually make things worse. If someone presents with manic or mixed symptoms, the priority is mood stabilization with appropriate antimanic treatments—not this combination.

faqs.q: What kind of monitoring should I expect if I start Symbyax?
faqs.a: You should expect: weight, BMI, and possibly waist circumference checks; fasting glucose or A1C and lipid panels; periodic liver function tests; basic electrolytes (especially sodium in older adults); movement checks for tremor or abnormal movements; and regular mood/suicidality assessments. If no one is monitoring these things, that’s a problem—bring it up.

faqs.q: How long do people usually stay on Symbyax?
faqs.a: It depends on why it was started and how you’re tolerating it. For acute bipolar depression or a severe TRD episode, many clinicians aim for months of stability before considering dose reduction or switching to something with a gentler metabolic profile. Long-term use is possible but should never be “set and forget”—periodically reassess whether you still need it, whether the dose can be reduced, or whether another option might give you similar mood benefits with fewer physical risks.
